opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's something I think about a lot, because there's a real tension. I'm not going to become a world-class expert in interpretability *and* adversarial robustness *and* scalable oversight *and* control all at once. There just isn't time, and the fields move too fast. But I also don't want to be in the position of purely deferring, where a senior researcher says "this is promising" and I just sign off on it.

So the standard I aim for is roughly this: I want to be able to tell a story, in my own words, about how a given line of research could end up mattering for reducing catastrophic risk from AI. Not a vague "this helps us understand models better," but something like: here's a specific failure mode we're worried about, maybe models that look aligned in training but pursue different goals when they get the chance, and here's how this project produces evidence or tools that make us more likely to catch or prevent that. If I can't articulate that chain, even roughly, I treat it as a sign that I either don't understand the work well enough or the theory of impact isn't there yet.

Beyond that, I try to understand the work well enough to have a reasonable sense of what success would look like and what would count as the research not panning out. Could I recognize a good result versus a disappointing one? Do I know what the main skeptics of this agenda would say, and do I have a view on whether they're right? That's often where the most useful learning happens, actually: talking to people who think a given agenda is a dead end and trying to understand their reasoning.

I'll be honest that I don't always hit that bar. Sometimes you're making a grant to a talented team whose work you understand at maybe a 60 percent level, and you're partly betting on the people. I think that's fine as long as you're honest with yourself that that's what you're doing. The thing I want to avoid is a kind of illusion of understanding, where you've absorbed the vocabulary of a research area without really being able to reason about it independently.

And part of what motivates the standard is that I think a grantmaker's job isn't just picking winners from a list. It's also noticing gaps, like "nobody is working on this thing that seems really important," and you can only do that if you have some internal model of the whole problem, not just a collection of opinions borrowed from different experts.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is something I think about a lot, because there's a real tension in grantmaking between how deep you can go on any one thing and how many things you need to cover. The standard I aspire to, and I want to be honest that I don't always hit it, is something like: I should be able to explain, in my own words, what the research direction is trying to accomplish, what the world looks like if it succeeds, and why that success would actually matter for the outcomes I care about, which is mostly reducing the chance that we lose control of very powerful AI systems.

Concretely, that means I want to be able to trace a chain from the technical work to the catastrophe it's supposed to help prevent. So if someone is working on, say, interpretability, I want to be able to say: okay, suppose this works really well in five years. What can we then do that we couldn't do before? Can we detect deceptive cognition in a model? Can we verify that a model isn't planning something we'd object to? And then, does that detection capability actually get used by the labs or governments at the moment when it matters? If I can't articulate that chain, or if the chain has a step where I'm just hand-waving, that's a signal that I don't understand the case for the grant well enough, even if the researchers are extremely credible.

The second piece is that I want to understand the project well enough to have a view on what the main ways it could fail are, and whether the researchers share that view. Not just "the research might not pan out," which is true of everything, but something more specific. Like, maybe the approach works on today's models but there's a reason to think it breaks down as models get more capable. Or maybe it produces a result that looks good on a benchmark but doesn't transfer to the adversarial setting where you'd actually need it. If I've talked to the team and they've thought about those failure modes more carefully than I have, that's a great sign. If I raise one and it seems new to them, that's informative too.

What I explicitly don't aspire to is being able to replicate or independently verify the technical work. I'm not going to be able to evaluate whether a particular training setup is implemented correctly or whether a proof goes through. That's where I lean on technical advisors and on the broader research community's reaction, and I think that's appropriate. The failure mode I'm trying to avoid is the one where I defer entirely, where I'm basically just pattern-matching on "this person is smart and says the words alignment" and funding on vibes. Because I think that's how a field ends up with a lot of work that's locally impressive but doesn't add up to anything.

And then the last thing I'd say is that the standard scales with the size of the bet. For a small exploratory grant, I'm okay with the chain being more speculative, with the understanding being "I can see how this could be important and the cost of finding out is low." For a large, multi-year commitment that's going to shape what a bunch of researchers work on, I want to have really pressure-tested the theory of change, ideally with people who disagree with it. I've been wrong before in both directions, funding things I understood too shallowly and passing on things I didn't take the time to understand, so I try to hold the standard seriously without pretending I've fully achieved it.

r001.rationale: The response says she wants to trace the theory of change, understand specific failure modes, and pressure-test large grants with people who disagree. It does not state a standard of anticipating and answering a wide range of intelligent criticisms.

r002.rationale: The response mentions balancing depth against breadth in grantmaking, but does not say her justification should go beyond the outside-view case for funding a diverse range of approaches.

astra-6.text:
I aspire to understand the argument well enough that I can explain it in my own words and push on the assumptions that matter. What problem is this work trying to solve? Why do we expect that problem to arise in advanced AI systems? And if the project succeeds, how does that actually help?

That doesn’t mean I need to be able to do the research myself or understand every technical detail. But I’d like to have more than a sense that the researcher is smart and other people think the work is promising. I want a concrete picture of how it could make things safer, where that picture is uncertain, and what we might learn that would change my mind.

That’s an aspiration, though. In practice, there’s going to be some reliance on other people’s judgment. The important thing is to distinguish the parts I understand from the parts where I’m deferring.

r001.rationale: The response says Cotra wants to explain the argument and probe important assumptions, but it does not state that she aims to anticipate and answer a wide range of intelligent criticisms.

r002.rationale: The response calls for a concrete safety rationale beyond others’ endorsements, but it does not identify the outside-view case for funding a diverse range of approaches.

sol-6.1.text:
I aspire to understand the theory of change well enough that I can explain, in my own words, how the research could make advanced AI safer, and what assumptions have to hold for that to work. What problem are we trying to solve? Why is this approach promising? And what would we learn from the project even if it doesn’t succeed?

That doesn’t mean I need to be able to do all the technical work myself. I’m going to rely on researchers’ judgment about a lot of things. But I want to understand where I’m relying on that judgment, rather than having a vague sense that something sounds important. Ideally, I can say what would change my mind and distinguish an exciting technical result from a result that actually advances the safety argument.
